notes.meaning: The record lists the twelve sons of Jacob, whom God named Israel. All twelve brothers formed the foundation of God's covenant nation. Dan is listed earlier than usual, placed right before Rachel's natural sons Joseph and Benjamin.

Judah is listed first among the brothers because the royal ruling family and the promised Messiah would come from his tribe. Er, Judah's oldest son, was put to death directly by God because of his evil actions. The line of Israel's kings began with real human weakness and God's holy judgment on sin.

Judah had twin sons, Perez and Zerah, through his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar. Even through a painful family scandal, God carried forward the family line that led toward King David through Perez. This shows that God's saving purposes continue even in the middle of human brokenness.
Perez had two sons named Hezron and Hamul. Hezron became the vital link in the family line leading directly to David. Hamul is recorded here to complete the record of the family branches.

Zerah had five sons who became renowned for their wisdom in ancient Israel. Later in Scripture, King Solomon was compared to four of these brothers to demonstrate how exceptionally wise he was. They were remembered as a great honor to their family name.

Carmi descended from Zerah through Zimri, and his son was Achar, also known as Achan. He is called Achar, which means 'troubler', because he stole goods at Jericho that were devoted entirely to God. His unfaithfulness brought sudden defeat and distress upon the whole nation until the wrong was addressed.

Ethan, one of Zerah's wise sons, had a son named Azariah. The writer mentions him briefly and does not trace his family any further. The main story leaves Zerah's line here because the royal rulers did not come from his branch.

Hezron had three main sons while living in Egypt: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb, who is also called Chelubai. Each of these three sons grew into a major family clan within the tribe of Judah. The family line of Ram is highlighted next because it leads to King David.

This line traces the ancestors of David through six generations, from Ram down to Jesse. Nahshon served as the chief prince of the tribe of Judah during the Exodus from Egypt. The line continued through Salmon, Boaz, and Obed, finally reaching Jesse in Bethlehem.

Jesse had seven sons listed here, with David named as the seventh and youngest. Although earlier biblical history mentions eight sons of Jesse, one son likely died young without having children. The number seven may also symbolize that David was chosen by God as the ideal king.

David had two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail, whose sons became powerful warriors in Israel's history. Zeruiah's three sons served as chief military commanders under David, while Abigail's son Amasa later led an army as well. Abigail's husband Jether lived among the Ishmaelites or had family ties to them.

The record moves to Caleb son of Hezron, who was an early ancestor and not the famous spy Caleb son of Jephunneh. He had children with his wives Azubah and Jerioth. The sons born to Azubah were Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.

After Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath and had a son named Hur. Hur's grandson was Bezalel, through his son Uri. God chose Bezalel and filled him with His Spirit as the master craftsman to build the tabernacle, Israel's tent of worship.

When Hezron was sixty years old, he married the daughter of Machir, the chief leader of Gilead from the tribe of Manasseh. She gave birth to Segub, who became the father of Jair. Jair held twenty-three towns in the region of Gilead, linking families from both Judah and Manasseh.

The kingdoms of Geshur and Aram eventually captured Jair's villages along with Kenath and its sixty surrounding settlements. All these towns originally belonged to the extended family of Machir, the leader of Gilead. Jair's family was counted as part of Machir's household because they settled there and defended the land together.

Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah, a region connected to his son Caleb and Caleb's wife Ephrath. After Hezron's death, his widow Abijah gave birth to a son named Ashhur. Ashhur is remembered as the father of Tekoa because he either founded the town or served as its chief ruler.

The family record turns to Jerahmeel, the oldest son of Hezron. His firstborn son was named Ram, sharing the name of Jerahmeel's brother, along with four other sons. Jerahmeel also had a second wife named Atarah, who became the mother of Onam.

Ram, the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, had three sons named Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. The Bible does not follow their lines any further into later history. Recording their names preserved an accurate tribal registry for Israel after the exile.

Onam, the son of Jerahmeel by Atarah, had two sons named Shammai and Jada. Shammai's family is then introduced to show how his branch of the clan grew. Including these lesser-known families showed that every household had a valued place among God's people.
